title: Taylor Chapter 13: Hamiltonian Mechanics
text:
According to the PHY C54 Syllabus, Hamiltonian Mechanics spans Week 04 (Ch 13: 1–4) and Week 05 (Ch 13: 5–7), concluding before Test #1.



The Legendre Transformation: Transitioning from generalized velocities \(\dot{q}_i\) to generalized canonical momenta \(p_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\).
Hamilton’s Canonical Equations: \[ \dot{q}_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{H}}{\partial p_i}, \quad \dot{p}_i = -\frac{\partial \mathcal{H}}{\partial q_i} \]
Phase Space Geometry & Liouville’s Theorem: Incompressibility of phase space volume under Hamiltonian time evolution (\(\frac{d\rho}{dt} = 0\)).
Poisson Brackets: Fundamental brackets, equations of motion in Poisson form, and canonical invariance: \[ [F, G] = \sum_i \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial G}{\partial p_i} - \frac{\partial F}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial G}{\partial q_i} \right) \]
Noether’s Theorem in Hamiltonian Mechanics: Symmetries, generators of infinitesimal canonical transformations, and conservation laws.

title: Taylor Chapter 10: Rotational Motion of Rigid Bodies
text:
According to the PHY C54 Syllabus, Rigid Body Dynamics is studied in Weeks 09, 10, and 11 (Taylor Ch 10: 1–10), following Test #2.



Center of Mass & Angular Momentum: \(\mathbf{L} = \sum_\alpha \mathbf{r}_\alpha \times \mathbf{p}_\alpha = \mathbf{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}\).

title: Taylor Chapter 7: Lagrange’s Equations
text:
The theoretical development of the laws of motion found its most poetic formulation in 1788 when the Italian-French mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange published Mécanique Analytique.
The Lagrangian formulation holds two major advantages over Newtonian mechanics: 1. Lagrange’s equations take the same form in any coordinate system (Cartesian, spherical, non-inertial, etc.). 2. For constrained systems (like a bead on a wire), the Lagrangian approach naturally eliminates the forces of constraint (like normal forces), which are often unknown and uninteresting.



(See Problems 7.1-7.7)
For a particle moving freely in 3D subject to a conservative force \(\mathbf{F} = -\nabla U\), the Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}\) is defined as the kinetic energy minus the potential energy: \[ \mathcal{L} = T - U = \frac{1}{2}m(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 + \dot{z}^2) - U(x, y, z) \]
By checking the partial derivatives, we see that: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = -\frac{\partial U}{\partial x} = F_x, \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{x}} = m\dot{x} = p_x \] Newton’s second law (\(F_x = \dot{p}_x\)) is therefore exactly equivalent to the Lagrange equation in Cartesian coordinates: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{x}} = 0 \]


Because this has the exact form of the Euler-Lagrange equations, we can re-state Newton’s Second Law as an integral variational principle known as Hamilton’s Principle: > The actual path which a particle follows between two points 1 and 2 in a given time interval makes the action integral \(S = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \mathcal{L} \, dt\) stationary.
Because Hamilton’s Principle applies globally to the action integral \(S\), the value of the integral is invariant under coordinate transformations. This proves that Lagrange’s equations are valid in any choice of generalized coordinates \(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n\).



If we write \(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m(\dot{r}^2 + r^2 \dot{\theta}^2) - U(r, \theta)\), the \(\theta\) equation becomes: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}} \implies -\frac{\partial U}{\partial \theta} = \frac{d}{dt} (mr^2 \dot{\theta}) \] Since \(-\partial U/\partial \theta\) is the torque \(\Gamma\) and \(mr^2\dot{\theta}\) is the angular momentum \(L\), this automatically yields \(\Gamma = \dot{L}\). The geometry of the coordinates naturally yields the appropriate mechanical theorem.





(See Problems 7.9-7.11)
A system of \(N\) particles with positions \(\mathbf{r}_\alpha\) is parametrized by generalized coordinates \(q_1, \dots, q_n\): \[ \mathbf{r}_\alpha = \mathbf{r}_\alpha(q_1, \dots, q_n, t) \]

Degrees of Freedom: The number of independently variable coordinates \(n\). If \(n < 3N\), the system is constrained.
Holonomic Systems: When the number of degrees of freedom exactly matches the number of generalized coordinates required to describe the configuration, the system is holonomic. (A rolling ball is non-holonomic, as it needs 5 coordinates but only has 2 translational degrees of freedom).
Natural Coordinates: If the transformation mapping \(\mathbf{r}_\alpha(q_1, \dots, q_n)\) does not depend explicitly on time \(t\), the coordinates are called “natural”.





(See Problems 7.12-7.13)
For a particle constrained to a surface (e.g., a bead on a wire), the total force is \(\mathbf{F}_{tot} = \mathbf{F}_{cstr} + \mathbf{F}\). The constraint force \(\mathbf{F}_{cstr}\) acts normal to the surface, and any virtual displacement \(\epsilon\) consistent with the constraint lies within the surface. Thus, \(\mathbf{F}_{cstr} \cdot \epsilon = 0\).
This geometric fact means the constraint forces do zero virtual work, entirely vanishing from the variation of the action \(\delta S = 0\). The resulting path requires only the potential \(U\) of the non-constraint forces: \[ \mathcal{L}(q, \dot{q}, t) = T - U \] yielding the \(n\) equations of motion: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} = 0 \quad \text{for } i = 1, \dots, n \]




(See Problems 7.14-7.44)
The procedure is nearly infallible: 1. Choose \(n\) generalized coordinates. 2. Write \(T\) and \(U\) in an inertial frame, then express them in terms of the \(q\)’s and \(\dot{q}\)’s. 3. Construct \(\mathcal{L} = T - U\). 4. Evaluate the Lagrange equations.


Consider a circular wire hoop of radius \(R\) spinning at constant angular velocity \(\omega\) about its vertical axis, with a bead of mass \(m\) free to slide. The generalized coordinate is the angle \(\theta\) from the bottom.
\[ \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}mR^2(\dot{\theta}^2 + \omega^2 \sin^2 \theta) - mgR(1 - \cos \theta) \] The equation of motion is: \[ R\ddot{\theta} = (\omega^2 R \cos \theta - g) \sin \theta \]
When \(\omega^2 < g/R\), the only stable equilibrium is at the bottom (\(\theta=0\)). But when the hoop spins fast enough (\(\omega^2 > g/R\)), the bottom becomes an unstable equilibrium, and two new stable equilibria emerge at \(\theta = \pm \arccos(g / \omega^2 R)\). This emergence is known in chaos theory as a pitchfork bifurcation.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

theta = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 200)
R = 1.0
g = 9.81

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
for w_sq in [5, 9.81, 20, 40]:
    force = (w_sq * R * np.cos(theta) - g) * np.sin(theta)
    plt.plot(theta, force, label=rf'$\omega^2={w_sq}$')

plt.axhline(0, color='k', linestyle='--', linewidth=0.8)
plt.title("Restoring Force vs. Angle $\\theta$")
plt.xlabel("$\\theta$ (radians)")
plt.ylabel("Normalized Force")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()








Figure 1: The effective restoring force on the spinning hoop bead. Note the stable equilibria moving away from the origin as rotation rate increases.










We define the generalized force \(F_i\) and generalized momentum \(p_i\) as: \[ F_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i} \quad \text{and} \quad p_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} \] Lagrange’s equations become exactly \(F_i = \dot{p}_i\).
Ignorable Coordinates: If \(\mathcal{L}\) is independent of a coordinate \(q_k\), we call \(q_k\) ignorable or cyclic. Its generalized force \(F_k = 0\), meaning the conjugate momentum \(p_k\) is strictly conserved! Every ignorable coordinate points to a conservation law.




(See Problems 7.45-7.47)


If an isolated system is translationally invariant (meaning \(\mathcal{L}\) doesn’t change if we shift all particles by an infinitesimal vector \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\)), it follows directly from Lagrange’s equations that the total linear momentum \(\mathbf{P} = \sum \mathbf{p}_\alpha\) is conserved.



The total time derivative of \(\mathcal{L}\) leads us to define the Hamiltonian \(\mathcal{H}\): \[ \mathcal{H} = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \dot{q}_i - \mathcal{L} \]
If the Lagrangian has no explicit time dependence (\(\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial t = 0\)), then \(d\mathcal{H}/dt = 0\), and the Hamiltonian is conserved. Furthermore, if the generalized coordinates are natural (time-independent transformations), Euler’s homogeneous function theorem guarantees that the kinetic energy \(T\) is a homogeneous quadratic function of the velocities, which implies: \[ \sum_{i} p_i \dot{q}_i = 2T \implies \mathcal{H} = 2T - (T - U) = T + U = E \] Hence, time-translation invariance leads to Energy Conservation.





(See Problems 7.48-7.49)
For a charged particle \(q\) in an electromagnetic field described by a scalar potential \(V\) and vector potential \(\mathbf{A}\), the Lorentz force is velocity-dependent: \(\mathbf{F} = q(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\).
The Lagrangian formulation still works if we adopt a generalized definition of the Lagrangian—a Lagrangian is simply any scalar function \(\mathcal{L}\) that reproduces the correct equations of motion.
For the electromagnetic case, the correct function is: \[ \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}m\dot{\mathbf{r}}^2 - q(V - \dot{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \mathbf{A}) \] This Lagrangian is foundational to quantum mechanics, as it modifies the canonical generalized momentum of the particle: \[ \mathbf{p} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{r}}} = m\mathbf{v} + q\mathbf{A} \] This shows that the momentum operator in quantum mechanics corresponds to \(m\mathbf{v} + q\mathbf{A}\), not just the mechanical momentum \(m\mathbf{v}\).




(See Problems 7.50-7.52)
If we need to determine a constraint force (e.g. tension in a string, or structural stress on a roller coaster track), we deliberately don’t use a minimal set of coordinates. Instead, we retain extra coordinates tied by a constraint equation \(f(q_1, q_2) = \text{const}\).
We introduce a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda(t)\) to scale the constraint equation, modifying Hamilton’s principle: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} + \lambda \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i} = 0 \]
The extra term \(\lambda \frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}\) is precisely the \(i\)-th component of the force of constraint. Solving this system of differential algebraic equations (DAEs) yields both the trajectory \(q_i(t)\) and the dynamic magnitude of the constraint force via \(\lambda(t)\).

title: Vector Calculus & Identities
text:

\[ \mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B} = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z = |\mathbf{A}| |\mathbf{B}| \cos\theta \] \[ \mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B} = \det \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{\hat{i}} & \mathbf{\hat{j}} & \mathbf{\hat{k}} \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix} \] \[ |\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}| = |\mathbf{A}| |\mathbf{B}| \sin\theta \]

title: Computational Methods for Mechanics
text:
In classical mechanics, analytic solutions are often impossible for systems that exhibit nonlinear dynamics, chaos, or lack conservation laws (e.g., the double pendulum, the 3-body problem, or driven damped oscillators). For these, we rely on numerical integration of Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs).
Any \(n\)-th order ODE can be reduced to a system of \(n\) first-order ODEs. For Newton’s second law \(\ddot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}, t)/m\), we define the state vector \(\mathbf{Y} = [\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}]^T\): \[ \frac{d\mathbf{Y}}{dt} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ \mathbf{a} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ \mathbf{F}/m \end{bmatrix} \]

title: Computational Methods for Mechanics
text:
The Velocity Verlet Method
Used extensively in molecular dynamics and astrophysics: 1. Update position by a half-step and full-step acceleration: \[ \mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n + \mathbf{v}_n \Delta t + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}_n \Delta t^2 \] 2. Calculate new forces/accelerations based on new position: \[ \mathbf{a}_{n+1} = \frac{1}{m} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) \] 3. Update velocity using the average of old and new accelerations: \[ \mathbf{v}_{n+1} = \mathbf{v}_n + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a}_n + \mathbf{a}_{n+1}) \Delta t \]


Code
import numpy as np

def velocity_verlet(x0, v0, force_func, m, dt, steps):
    x = np.zeros(steps)
    v = np.zeros(steps)
    x[0], v[0] = x0, v0
    
    a = force_func(x0) / m
    for i in range(steps - 1):
        x[i+1] = x[i] + v[i]*dt + 0.5*a*dt**2
        a_next = force_func(x[i+1]) / m
        v[i+1] = v[i] + 0.5*(a + a_next)*dt
        a = a_next
        
    return x, v

The integral to evaluate from Equation (6.23) is: \[x = \int \sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} \, dy\]
Taylor introduces the substitution: \[y = a(1 - \cos\theta)\]


Differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(\theta\): \[dy = \frac{d}{d\theta}\big[a(1 - \cos\theta)\big] d\theta = a\sin\theta \, d\theta\] Using the double-angle identity \(\sin\theta = 2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\): \[dy = 2a \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) d\theta\]



Substitute \(y = a(1 - \cos\theta)\) into the numerator and denominator under the radical: Numerator: \[y = a(1 - \cos\theta) = 2a\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\] Denominator: \[2a - y = 2a - a(1 - \cos\theta) = a(1 + \cos\theta) = 2a\cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\] Taking the ratio inside the square root: \[\frac{y}{2a - y} = \frac{2a\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{2a\cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)} = \tan^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\] Assuming the motion stays within the first arch (\(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\) where \(\theta/2 \in [0, \pi]\) and \(\sin(\theta/2) \ge 0\)): \[\sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} = \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}\]



Multiply the simplified radical by \(dy\): \[\sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} \, dy = \left(\frac{\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}\right) \cdot \left[2a \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) d\theta\right] = 2a \sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) d\theta\] Recall the half-angle identity \(2\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = 1 - \cos\theta\): \[x = \int a(1 - \cos\theta) \, d\theta = a(\theta - \sin\theta) + C\] Applying the initial condition \(x(0) = 0\) gives \(C = 0\), recovering the cycloid parametric equations: \[x = a(\theta - \sin\theta), \quad y = a(1 - \cos\theta)\]

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
section: 1. Euler’s First and Third Substitutions for \(\sqrt{Ax^2 + Bx + C}\)
text:
1. Euler’s First and Third Substitutions for \(\sqrt{Ax^2 + Bx + C}\)
When quadratic radicands cannot be cleanly solved by simple trigonometric substitution or completing the square, Euler’s algebraic substitutions rationalize the integral by establishing a birational map between the conic \(Y^2 = Ax^2 + Bx + C\) and a parameter \(t\):

Euler’s First Substitution (\(A > 0\))

Condition: The leading coefficient \(A\) is positive.
Substitution: \[ \sqrt{Ax^2 + Bx + C} = \pm \sqrt{A}x + t \]
Derivation: Square both sides: \[ Ax^2 + Bx + C = Ax^2 \pm 2\sqrt{A}xt + t^2 \implies Bx + C = \pm 2\sqrt{A}xt + t^2 \] Notice that \(Ax^2\) cancels completely! Solving for \(x\) yields a purely rational expression in \(t\): \[ x = \frac{t^2 - C}{B \mp 2\sqrt{A}t} \] Both \(x\) and \(dx = \frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac{t^2 - C}{B \mp 2\sqrt{A}t}\right]dt\), as well as the radical itself, become rational functions of \(t\). The integral is completely solved by partial fractions.



Euler’s Third Substitution (Real Roots \(r_1, r_2\))

Condition: The quadratic factors over the reals as \(Ax^2 + Bx + C = A(x - r_1)(x - r_2)\).
Substitution: \[ \sqrt{A(x - r_1)(x - r_2)} = t(x - r_1) \]
Derivation: Square both sides: \[ A(x - r_1)(x - r_2) = t^2(x - r_1)^2 \] Divide by \((x - r_1)\): \[ A(x - r_2) = t^2(x - r_1) \implies Ax - A r_2 = t^2 x - t^2 r_1 \implies x = \frac{A r_2 - t^2 r_1}{A - t^2} \] The radical simplifies to \(t(x - r_1) = \frac{A(r_2 - r_1)t}{A - t^2}\), rendering the integrand completely rational in \(t\).

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
text:
2. The Weierstrass Tangent Half-Angle Substitution
The Weierstrass substitution is known as the “universal trigonometric substitution.” It algebraically transforms any rational expression of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) into a rational polynomial integral:

Geometric Origin
Consider the unit circle \(X^2 + Y^2 = 1\) parameterized by the angle \(\theta\) where \((X, Y) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\). Draw a secant line from the fixed point \((-1, 0)\) through \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) to the vertical line \(X = 0\). The slope of this line is: \[ t = \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \] By stereographic projection, every point on the unit circle corresponds to a unique real slope \(t \in (-\infty, \infty)\).


Algebraic Formulas
Using standard double-angle formulas with \(\tan(\theta/2) = t\): \[ \cos\theta = \cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) - \sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{\cos^2(\theta/2) - \sin^2(\theta/2)}{\cos^2(\theta/2) + \sin^2(\theta/2)} = \frac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2} \] \[ \sin\theta = 2\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)}{\cos^2(\theta/2) + \sin^2(\theta/2)} = \frac{2t}{1 + t^2} \] Differentiating \(\theta = 2\arctan(t)\): \[ d\theta = \frac{2}{1 + t^2} \, dt \]


Example
To evaluate \(\int \frac{d\theta}{2 + \cos\theta}\): \[ \int \frac{\frac{2\, dt}{1 + t^2}}{2 + \frac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}} = \int \frac{2\, dt}{2(1 + t^2) + (1 - t^2)} = \int \frac{2\, dt}{3 + t^2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + C = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan\left(\frac{\tan(\theta/2)}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + C \]

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
section: 3. Hyperbolic Conversions for Catenaries and Relativistic Rapidity
text:
3. Hyperbolic Conversions for Catenaries and Relativistic Rapidity
Whenever variational problems produce forms like \(\int \frac{dy}{\sqrt{y^2 - y_0^2}}\):

Why Hyperbolic Beats Trigonometric Secant

If you use trigonometric secant \(y = y_0\sec\theta\): \[ \int \frac{y_0\sec\theta\tan\theta}{\sqrt{y_0^2(\sec^2\theta - 1)}} \, d\theta = \int \sec\theta \, d\theta = \ln|\sec\theta + \tan\theta| + C = \ln\left|\frac{y + \sqrt{y^2 - y_0^2}}{y_0}\right| + C \] Inverting this logarithm to isolate \(y(x)\) requires exponentiation and solving quadratic equations with annoying sign choices.
Using hyperbolic cosine \(y = y_0\cosh u \implies dy = y_0\sinh u \, du\): \[ \int \frac{y_0\sinh u}{\sqrt{y_0^2(\cosh^2 u - 1)}} \, du = \int \frac{y_0\sinh u}{y_0\sinh u} \, du = \int du = u + C = \operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{y}{y_0}\right) + C \] Inverting this immediately gives: \[ y(x) = y_0\cosh\left(\frac{x - x_0}{y_0}\right) \] in a single clean step, eliminating absolute values and logarithms.



Application to Relativistic Rapidity
In special relativity, velocity addition is non-linear: \(v_{13} = \frac{v_{12} + v_{23}}{1 + v_{12}v_{23}/c^2}\).
By defining rapidity \(\eta = \operatorname{artanh}(v/c)\), velocity addition becomes strictly linear: \[ \eta_{13} = \eta_{12} + \eta_{23} \] The Lorentz factor becomes \(\gamma = \cosh\eta\), the momentum becomes \(p = mc\sinh\eta\), and the relativistic kinetic energy integral \(\int v\, dp = mc^2\int \tanh\eta\cosh\eta\, d\eta = mc^2\int \sinh\eta\, d\eta = mc^2(\cosh\eta - 1) = (\gamma - 1)mc^2\) is evaluated instantly.

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
text:
Problem 1: The Normalized Fractional Root
\[\int_0^1 \sqrt{\frac{x}{1-x}} \, dx\]
Target Trick: The half-angle cycloid substitution (\(x = \sin^2\theta\)).
Speed-Round Solution: Let \(x = \sin^2\theta\), so \(dx = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\, d\theta\). The bounds transform as \(0 \to 0\) and \(1 \to \pi/2\): \[\sqrt{\frac{x}{1-x}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}} = \tan\theta\] Substitute directly into the integral: \[\int_0^{\pi/2} (\tan\theta) \cdot (2\sin\theta\cos\theta)\, d\theta = 2 \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^2\theta\, d\theta\] Using the average value of \(\sin^2\theta\) over a quarter-period: \[2 \left(\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \mathbf{\frac{\pi}{2}}\]

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
text:
Problem 2: The Factored Quadratic Surd
\[\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{(x+1)\sqrt{x(1-x)}}\]
Target Trick: Euler’s third substitution / factored root normalization.
Speed-Round Solution: Substitute \(x = \sin^2\theta\), giving \(dx = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\, d\theta\) and \(\sqrt{x(1-x)} = \sin\theta\cos\theta\): \[\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta\, d\theta}{(1 + \sin^2\theta)\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{2\, d\theta}{1 + \sin^2\theta}\] Divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^2\theta\) to prepare an algebraic substitution: \[\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{2\sec^2\theta}{\sec^2\theta + \tan^2\theta}\, d\theta = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{2\sec^2\theta}{1 + 2\tan^2\theta}\, d\theta\] Substitute \(u = \sqrt{2}\tan\theta\), so \(du = \sqrt{2}\sec^2\theta\, d\theta\), with limits \(0 \to \infty\): \[\int_0^\infty \frac{\sqrt{2}\, du}{1 + u^2} = \sqrt{2} \left[ \arctan(u) \right]_0^\infty = \sqrt{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \mathbf{\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}}\]

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
text:
Problem 3: The 15-Second Weierstrass Benchmark
\[\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{dx}{1 + \sin x + \cos x}\]
Target Trick: The classic half-angle substitution \(t = \tan(x/2)\).
Speed-Round Solution: Recall the rational identities: \[\sin x = \frac{2t}{1+t^2}, \quad \cos x = \frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}, \quad dx = \frac{2\, dt}{1+t^2}\] Combine the denominator terms: \[1 + \sin x + \cos x = \frac{(1+t^2) + 2t + (1-t^2)}{1+t^2} = \frac{2(1+t)}{1+t^2}\] The \((1+t^2)\) factors cancel against \(dx\): \[\int_0^1 \frac{\frac{2\, dt}{1+t^2}}{\frac{2(1+t)}{1+t^2}} = \int_0^1 \frac{dt}{1+t} = \left[ \ln(1+t) \right]_0^1 = \mathbf{\ln 2}\]

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
text:
Problem 4: Inverse Factorization on \(\sqrt{x^2 - 1}\)
\[\int_1^2 \frac{\sqrt{x^2 - 1}}{x^4}\, dx\]
Target Trick: Direct radical factoring \(u = \sqrt{1 - x^{-2}}\) (bypassing trigonometric substitution).
Speed-Round Solution: Factor \(x\) out of the radical in the numerator: \[\frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{x^4} = \frac{x\sqrt{1 - x^{-2}}}{x^4} = \frac{\sqrt{1 - x^{-2}}}{x^3}\] Set \(u = \sqrt{1 - x^{-2}}\). Then \(u^2 = 1 - x^{-2} \implies 2u\, du = 2x^{-3}\, dx\), so: \[\frac{dx}{x^3} = u\, du\] The bounds transform from \(x \in [1, 2]\) to \(u \in \left[0, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right]\): \[\int_0^{\sqrt{3}/2} u \cdot (u\, du) = \int_0^{\sqrt{3}/2} u^2\, du = \left[ \frac{u^3}{3} \right]_0^{\sqrt{3}/2} = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{8}\right) = \mathbf{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{8}}\]

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
text:
Problem 5: Hyperbolic Shift with Inversion
\[\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{(x+1)\sqrt{x^2 + 2x + 2}}\]
Target Trick: Completing the square followed by inversion substitution \(u = 1/t\).
Speed-Round Solution: Complete the square inside the radical: \(x^2 + 2x + 2 = (x+1)^2 + 1\). Shift variables with \(y = x+1\): \[\int_1^2 \frac{dy}{y\sqrt{y^2 + 1}}\] Apply the inversion substitution \(y = \frac{1}{t}\), which gives \(dy = -\frac{dt}{t^2}\): \[\int_1^{1/2} \frac{-\frac{dt}{t^2}}{\frac{1}{t}\sqrt{\frac{1}{t^2} + 1}} = \int_{1/2}^1 \frac{dt}{\sqrt{1 + t^2}}\] Using the standard anti-derivative \(\int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{1+t^2}} = \operatorname{arsinh}(t) = \ln(t + \sqrt{t^2+1})\): \[\left[ \ln\left(t + \sqrt{t^2 + 1}\right) \right]_{1/2}^1 = \ln(1 + \sqrt{2}) - \ln\left(\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right) = \mathbf{\ln\left(\frac{2 + 2\sqrt{2}}{1 + \sqrt{5}}\right)}\]

Imagine a circular disk of radius \(a\) rolling without slipping along the underside of the horizontal axis (\(y = 0\), pointing downward):
Center of the wheel: As the wheel rolls through an angle \(\theta\), its contact point has rolled a distance \(a\theta\) along the rail. The center of the disk is located at: \[(x_c, y_c) = (a\theta, a)\]
Point on the perimeter (\(P\)): A marker fixed to the rim starts at the origin \((0, 0)\) when \(\theta = 0\). After rotating clockwise by \(\theta\), the marker’s relative displacement from the wheel’s center is: \[\Delta x = -a\sin\theta, \quad \Delta y = -a\cos\theta\]
Absolute coordinates: Combining center translation and rim rotation yields the parametric equations: \[x(\theta) = x_c + \Delta x = a(\theta - \sin\theta)\] \[y(\theta) = y_c + \Delta y = a(1 - \cos\theta)\]
\(\theta\) also directly determines the local slope and launch angle of the path. Differentiating with respect to \(\theta\): \[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta} = \frac{a\sin\theta}{a(1 - \cos\theta)} = \frac{2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)}{2\sin^2(\theta/2)} = \cot\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\]
If \(\psi\) is the inclination angle of the velocity vector relative to the horizontal (\(\tan\psi = dy/dx\)): \[\psi = \frac{\pi - \theta}{2}\] - At \(\theta \to 0\) (the start): \(\psi = \pi/2\) (the path drops straight vertically). - At \(\theta = \pi\) (the trough): \(\psi = 0\) (the trajectory is completely horizontal). - At \(\theta = 2\pi\) (the next cusp): \(\psi = -\pi/2\) (the path rises back to vertical).

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
section: Why Assume the First Arch (\(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\)) and \(\sin(\theta/2) \ge 0\)?
text:
Why Assume the First Arch (\(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\)) and \(\sin(\theta/2) \ge 0\)?

1. The Mathematical Reason: Eliminating Absolute Value Signs
The substitution replaces \(\sqrt{y / (2a - y)}\) with trigonometric functions: \[\sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} = \sqrt{\frac{2a\sin^2(\theta/2)}{2a\cos^2(\theta/2)}} = \sqrt{\tan^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)} = \left\vert{} \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \right\vert{} = \frac{\left\vert{}\sin(\theta/2)\right\vert{}}{\left\vert{}\cos(\theta/2)\right\vert{}}\] By definition, the principal square root \(\sqrt{u^2} = \vert{}u\vert{}\). If \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\), then the half-angle satisfies \(\frac{\theta}{2} \in [0, \pi]\). The sine function is strictly non-negative across the entire interval \([0, \pi]\): \[\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \ge 0 \implies \left\vert{}\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right\vert{} = \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\] This ensures that the integrand evaluates to \(\sin(\theta/2)\) without carrying piece-wise \(\pm\) absolute value signs.


2. The Physical Reason: Geometry of the Fastest Path

Energy Bounds: Conservation of mechanical energy gives \(v = \sqrt{2gy}\). At \(y = 0\), speed is zero (\(v = 0\)). The particle cannot rise above \(y = 0\), which means it cannot continue past a cusp into negative \(y\).
Uniqueness: A single arch (\(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\)) starts at \((0, 0)\) and terminates at \((2\pi a, 0)\). By scaling the radius \(a\), a single cycloid arch can pass through any target point \((x_2, y_2)\) in the lower half-plane (\(x_2 > 0, y_2 \ge 0\)).
No Redundant Loops: Any path extending past \(\theta = 2\pi\) into a second arch would involve rising up to a cusp, stopping, and dropping into a new dip. That would add unnecessary path length and travel time, violating the time-minimization condition \(\delta T = 0\).

title: Integration Tricks and Substitution Techniques
text:
Essential Mathematical Properties of Cycloids
Parametric Form: \[x(\theta) = a(\theta - \sin\theta), \quad y(\theta) = a(1 - \cos\theta)\]
Differential Arc Length: \[ds = \sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2}\, d\theta = a\sqrt{(1-\cos\theta)^2 + \sin^2\theta}\, d\theta = 2a\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) d\theta\]
Total Arc Length from Origin to \(\theta\): \[s(\theta) = \int_0^\theta 2a\sin\left(\frac{\theta'}{2}\right) d\theta' = 4a\left(1 - \cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right) = 8a\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{4}\right)\]
The total perimeter of one complete arch (\(\theta = 2\pi\)) is exactly: \[s_{\text{total}} = 8a\]
Radius of Curvature: \[\rho(\theta) = \frac{(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2)^{3/2}}{\vert{}\dot{x}\ddot{y} - \dot{y}\ddot{x}\vert{}} = 4a\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \sqrt{8a y}\]
Self-Evolute Property: The evolute (locus of centers of curvature) of a cycloid is an identical cycloid, shifted horizontally by \(\pi a\) and vertically downward by \(2a\).

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class DoublePendulumScene(Scene):
    def construct(self):
        title = Title("Double Pendulum: Hamiltonian Chaos", color=BLUE_B)
        self.play(Write(title))

        # Origin pivot
        origin = UP * 1.5
        pivot = Dot(origin, color=WHITE, radius=0.08)

        # Pendulum parameters
        l1, l2 = 2.0, 1.8
        theta1, theta2 = 120 * DEGREES, -45 * DEGREES

        # Calculate coordinates
        p1 = origin + l1 * np.array([np.sin(theta1), -np.cos(theta1), 0])
        p2 = p1 + l2 * np.array([np.sin(theta2), -np.cos(theta2), 0])

        rod1 = Line(origin, p1, color=GRAY_B, stroke_width=4)
        rod2 = Line(p1, p2, color=GRAY_B, stroke_width=4)

        bob1 = Dot(p1, color=RED, radius=0.15)
        bob2 = Dot(p2, color=YELLOW, radius=0.15)

        self.play(FadeIn(pivot), Create(rod1), Create(rod2), GrowFromCenter(bob1), GrowFromCenter(bob2))
        self.wait(1)

text:
Overview
The cycloid is one of the most celebrated curves in classical mechanics and the calculus of variations. Discovered by Galileo and investigated by Bernoulli, Newton, Leibniz, and Huygens, it possesses two remarkable variational properties:

The Brachistochrone: The path of fastest descent under uniform gravity between two points.
The Tautochrone (Isochrone): A curve along which a particle released from rest at any point reaches the bottom in the exact same time, independent of release height.
The Cycloidal Pendulum: By suspending a flexible pendulum string between two cycloidal guides (“cheeks”), the string unwraps along the cheeks so the bob traces an exact evolute cycloid, eliminating the “circular error” of ordinary pendulums.

Below are four live, interactive in-browser simulations demonstrating these principles.



Simulation 1: Generating a Cycloid — Rolling Wheel Along Underside of Axis
A cycloid is defined geometrically as the trajectory traced out by a fixed marker point on the rim of a wheel of radius \(a\) rolling without slipping along a straight line. In the Brachistochrone problem, the rail is the horizontal ceiling axis \(y = 0\), and the wheel rolls along its underside (\(y\) increasing downward):

Wheel Center: \((x_c, y_c) = (a\theta, a)\)
Rim Marker \(P(x, y)\): \(x(\theta) = a(\theta - \sin\theta), \quad y(\theta) = a(1 - \cos\theta)\)

Simulation 3: The Tautochrone (Isochrone) Property
Huygens discovered in 1659 that an inverted cycloid is tautochronous: a frictionless particle sliding down a cycloidal track to the lowest point takes the exact same time regardless of where on the arch it is released!
The equation of motion along the arc length \(s\) (measured from the trough) is pure simple harmonic motion: \[ \ddot{s} + \left(\frac{g}{4a}\right) s = 0 \] All beads reach the trough \(s = 0\) at the identical quarter-period mark: \[ t_{\text{trough}} = \pi \sqrt{\frac{a}{g}} \]

In a standard circular pendulum, the period increases with amplitude: \[ T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\left(1 + \frac{1}{16}\theta_0^2 + \frac{11}{3072}\theta_0^4 + \dots\right) \] This circular error caused grandfather clocks to lose time whenever the drive spring wound down and the swing amplitude decreased.
Christiaan Huygens eliminated this error in 1673 by flanking the suspension string with two curved metal guides shaped like cycloids (cycloidal cheeks). As the pendulum swings wide, the flexible string wraps against the cheek, shortening the effective radius of curvature and accelerating the bob just enough so that the trajectory of the bob is an exact evolute cycloid!
The period of Huygens’ cycloidal clock is strictly invariant across all amplitudes: \[ T_{\text{cycloid}} = 4\pi\sqrt{\frac{a}{g}} \]

text:
A bead of mass \(m\) slides without friction on a circular wire hoop of radius \(R\). The hoop rotates with a constant angular velocity \(\omega\) about its vertical diameter.

Construct the Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}(\theta, \dot{\theta})\).

title: Bead on a Rotating Wire Hoop Problem
text:
Solution

1. Constructing the Lagrangian
Let \(\theta\) be the angle of the bead measured from the lowest point of the hoop. In spherical coordinates with the origin at the center of the hoop: * \(x = R \sin\theta \cos(\omega t)\) * \(y = R \sin\theta \sin(\omega t)\) * \(z = -R \cos\theta\)
Taking time derivatives: \[\dot{x} = R \dot{\theta} \cos\theta \cos(\omega t) - R \omega \sin\theta \sin(\omega t)\] \[\dot{y} = R \dot{\theta} \cos\theta \sin(\omega t) + R \omega \sin\theta \cos(\omega t)\] \[\dot{z} = R \dot{\theta} \sin\theta\]
Calculating \(v^2 = \dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 + \dot{z}^2\): \[v^2 = R^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + R^2 \omega^2 \sin^2\theta\]

Kinetic Energy: \(T = \frac{1}{2} m R^2 (\dot{\theta}^2 + \omega^2 \sin^2\theta)\)
Potential Energy: \(V = mgz = -mgR \cos\theta\)

The Lagrangian is: \[\boxed{\mathcal{L} = T - V = \frac{1}{2} m R^2 \dot{\theta}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m R^2 \omega^2 \sin^2\theta + mgR \cos\theta}\]



2. Equation of Motion
Compute the Euler-Lagrange derivatives: \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}} = m R^2 \dot{\theta} \implies \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}}\right) = m R^2 \ddot{\theta}\] \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = m R^2 \omega^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta - mgR \sin\theta\]
Applying \(\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}} - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = 0\): \[m R^2 \ddot{\theta} - m R^2 \omega^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta + mgR \sin\theta = 0\] \[\boxed{\ddot{\theta} = \left( \omega^2 \cos\theta - \frac{g}{R} \right) \sin\theta}\]



3. Equilibrium Positions and Stability Analysis
Equilibrium occurs when \(\ddot{\theta} = 0\): \[\sin\theta \left( \omega^2 \cos\theta - \frac{g}{R} \right) = 0\]
This yields two distinct branches of equilibria: 1. \(\sin\theta = 0 \implies \theta_0 = 0\) (bottom) or \(\theta_0 = \pi\) (top). 2. \(\cos\theta_0 = \frac{g}{\omega^2 R}\) (lateral positions, existing only if \(\omega^2 \ge g/R\)).

Effective Potential
Rewrite the equation of motion as \(\ddot{\theta} = -\frac{1}{mR^2} \frac{dV_{\text{eff}}}{d\theta}\): \[V_{\text{eff}}(\theta) = -mgR \cos\theta - \frac{1}{2} m R^2 \omega^2 \sin^2\theta\]
Evaluate the second derivative \(\frac{d^2 V_{\text{eff}}}{d\theta^2}\): \[\frac{d^2 V_{\text{eff}}}{d\theta^2} = mgR \cos\theta - m R^2 \omega^2 \cos(2\theta)\]
At the bottom (\(\theta = 0\)): \[\left. \frac{d^2 V_{\text{eff}}}{d\theta^2} \right|_{\theta=0} = mgR - m R^2 \omega^2 = m R^2 \left( \frac{g}{R} - \omega^2 \right)\]

Subcritical (\(\omega < \sqrt{g/R}\)): \(V_{\text{eff}}''(0) > 0 \implies\) Stable minimum.
Supercritical (\(\omega > \sqrt{g/R}\)): \(V_{\text{eff}}''(0) < 0 \implies\) Unstable maximum. The bottom position loses stability!

At the critical rotation speed \(\omega_c = \sqrt{g/R}\), the system undergoes a classic supercritical pitchfork bifurcation: the bottom point becomes unstable, and two symmetric stable equilibrium points emerge at: \[\boxed{\theta_0 = \pm \arccos\left(\frac{g}{\omega^2 R}\right)}\]

The shortest path between two points on a curved surface, such as the surface of a sphere, is called a geodesic. To find a geodesic, one has first to set up an integral that gives the length of a path on the surface in question. Use spherical polar coordinates \((r, \theta, \phi)\) to show that the length of a path joining two points on a sphere of radius \(R\) is \[ L = R \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{1 + \sin^2\theta \ (\phi')^2} \, d\theta \] if \((\theta_1, \phi_1)\) and \((\theta_2, \phi_2)\) specify the two points and we assume that the path is expressed as \(\phi = \phi(\theta)\).


Problem 6.2
Find the equation of the path \(y(x)\) that makes the integral \(\int_{x_1}^{x_2} \sqrt{x} \sqrt{1 + (y')^2} \, dx\) stationary.


Problem 6.7
Verify that a straight line is the shortest distance between two points in a Euclidean plane. Set up the integral for the length of a path \(y(x)\) between two points \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\) and use the Euler-Lagrange equation to show that the minimizing path is \(y(x) = mx + c\).

3. High-Precision Python Integration & Phase Portraits
In Python, we utilize scipy.integrate.solve_ivp with the Dormand-Prince 8th order (DOP853) method to integrate the non-linear pendulum and plot its phase portrait:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

def pendulum_deriv(t, y, g=9.81, L=1.0):
    theta, omega = y
    return [omega, -(g / L) * np.sin(theta)]

t_span = (0, 20)
t_eval = np.linspace(0, 20, 1000)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

# Plot trajectories for several initial angles
for theta0 in [np.pi/6, np.pi/3, np.pi/2, 2.5, 3.1]:
    sol = solve_ivp(pendulum_deriv, t_span, [theta0, 0.0], t_eval=t_eval, method='DOP853')
    plt.plot(sol.y[0], sol.y[1], label=f"$\\theta_0 = {theta0:.2f}$ rad")

plt.title("Phase Space Trajectories ($\\theta$ vs $\\dot{\\theta}$)")
plt.xlabel("Angle $\\theta$ (rad)")
plt.ylabel("Angular Velocity $\\dot{\\theta}$ (rad/s)")
plt.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)
plt.axvline(x=np.pi, color='r', linestyle=':', label="Separatrix Saddle ($\\pm \\pi$)")
plt.axvline(x=-np.pi, color='r', linestyle=':')
plt.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.show()

For ultra-high-throughput orbital mechanics, Fortran remains an industry standard in celestial dynamics:

program kepler_verlet
    implicit none
    integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0)
    real(dp) :: x, y, vx, vy, ax, ay, r, dt, t, t_end, GM
    real(dp) :: ax_new, ay_new
    integer :: step, n_steps

    GM = 4.0_dp * 3.141592653589793_dp**2 ! AU^3 / yr^2
    x = 1.0_dp; y = 0.0_dp               ! Initial position (1 AU)
    vx = 0.0_dp; vy = 2.0_dp * 3.141592653589793_dp ! Circular velocity

    dt = 0.001_dp
    t_end = 10.0_dp
    n_steps = int(t_end / dt)

    do step = 1, n_steps
        r = sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
        ax = -GM * x / (r**3)
        ay = -GM * y / (r**3)

        x = x + vx * dt + 0.5_dp * ax * dt**2
        y = y + vy * dt + 0.5_dp * ay * dt**2

        r = sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
        ax_new = -GM * x / (r**3)
        ay_new = -GM * y / (r**3)

        vx = vx + 0.5_dp * (ax + ax_new) * dt
        vy = vy + 0.5_dp * (ay + ay_new) * dt
    end do

    print *, "Completed 10 Earth orbits with zero secular energy drift."
end program kepler_verlet

title: Formalizing Calculus of Variations in Lean 4
text:
In Chapter 6, we derived the Euler-Lagrange equations using the calculus of variations. While physicists often use heuristic arguments and physical intuition to define functional derivatives and stationary points, mathematicians require rigorous definitions involving Banach spaces, Fréchet derivatives, and functional analysis.
Lean 4 is a dependently typed functional programming language and interactive theorem prover. In recent years, it has gained immense popularity in academia (e.g., the Fields Medalist Peter Scholze’s Liquid Tensor Experiment, and Terrence Tao’s recent work) for formalizing complex mathematics.
In this article, we explore how the calculus of variations and the principle of stationary action can be formalized in Lean 4 using its mathematics library, mathlib.


To formalize the calculus of variations, we need a rigorous framework for calculus on infinite-dimensional spaces (spaces of paths/functions). In Lean 4, this is handled through the theory of Normed Spaces and Fréchet derivatives.
In mathlib, the derivative of a function \(f : E \to F\) between two normed vector spaces is defined using the HasFDerivAt or fderiv API.
import Mathlib.Analysis.Calculus.Deriv.Basic
import Mathlib.Analysis.NormedSpace.Basic

-- E and F are Normed Vector Spaces over ℝ
variable {E F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
variable [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]

-- A function f is differentiable at x if it has a continuous linear map as its Fréchet derivative
-- fderiv ℝ f x represents the Fréchet derivative of f at x
For the action functional \(S\), the domain \(E\) is a space of paths (e.g., a Sobolev space \(W^{1,2}\) or a space of smooth functions \(C^\infty([t_1, t_2], \mathbb{R}^n)\)), and the codomain \(F\) is \(\mathbb{R}\).



In physics, the action is: \[ S[q] = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} L(t, q(t), \dot{q}(t)) \, dt \]
To formalize this in Lean, we must: 1. Define the Lagrangian \(L : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) with appropriate smoothness conditions (e.g., \(C^2\)). 2. Define the space of admissible paths \(\mathcal{P} = \{ q \in C^2([t_1, t_2], \mathbb{R}^n) \mid q(t_1) = q_1, q(t_2) = q_2 \}\). 3. Define the integral using Lean’s measure theory library (Bochner integration).
import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Integral.Bochner

-- A rough sketch of how the action functional might be typed in Lean
def ActionFunctional (L : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ → ℝ) (q : ℝ → ℝ) (t1 t2 : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ t in t1..t2, L t (q t) (deriv q t)



The principle of stationary action states that the physical path \(q_{true}\) is a critical point of \(S[q]\): \[ \delta S = 0 \iff D S(q_{true})[\eta] = 0 \quad \text{for all variations } \eta \]
In Lean, stating that a function has a local extremum (or just a stationary point) involves asserting that its Fréchet derivative evaluates to zero. mathlib contains theorems like hasFDerivAt_of_local_min, which proves that the derivative is zero at a local minimum, generalizing Fermat’s theorem to Banach spaces.
theorem stationary_action (S : (ℝ → ℝ) → ℝ) (q : ℝ → ℝ)
    (h_stat : fderiv ℝ S q = 0) : 
    /- Euler-Lagrange equations hold -/ := by
  sorry -- The proof involves integration by parts, formalized via the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.



A crucial step in the physics derivation is the Fundamental Lemma of Calculus of Variations: If \(\int_{t_1}^{t_2} f(t) \eta(t) dt = 0\) for all smooth functions \(\eta(t)\) vanishing at the boundaries, then \(f(t) = 0\) everywhere.
Formalizing this lemma in Lean 4 requires: 1. Constructing bump functions (which are available in mathlib’s smooth manifolds library). 2. Using measure theory to show that if the integral of \(f \cdot \eta\) is zero for all bump functions, the almost-everywhere equivalence class of \(f\) is zero. 3. Using the continuity of \(f\) to upgrade “almost everywhere zero” to “everywhere zero”.



While the basic calculus of variations is well-understood mathematically, its complete, end-to-end formalization in Lean 4 is an active area of interest within the mathematical physics community:

Differential Geometry and Mechanics: The mathlib community is actively developing the theory of smooth manifolds, tangent bundles, and symplectic geometry. Classical mechanics naturally lives on the cotangent bundle \(T^*M\) (Hamiltonian mechanics) and the tangent bundle \(TM\) (Lagrangian mechanics).
Noether’s Theorem: Formalizing symmetry and conservation laws using Lie groups acting on manifolds is a major milestone for formalizing physics.
Optics & Shortest Paths: Formalizing that geodesics on a Riemannian manifold satisfy the geodesic equation (a special case of Euler-Lagrange) is closely tied to ongoing work in Riemannian geometry in Lean 4.

By translating physics into Lean 4, researchers can ensure there are no hidden assumptions in their derivations, providing absolute rigor to the foundational principles of mechanics we study in Chapter 6!

title: Physics and Engineering Applications of Cycloids
text:
The original problem posed by Johann Bernoulli in 1696: finding the frictionless track between two points under uniform gravity that minimizes total transit time: \[T = \int \frac{ds}{v} = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \sqrt{\frac{1 + y'^2}{2gy}}\, dx\] The solution is an inverted cycloid. Dropping vertically at first allows the particle to rapidly convert potential energy into kinetic energy (\(v = \sqrt{2gy}\)), maximizing ground speed early in the transit.



A simple pendulum with a circular swing is not strictly isochronous; its period depends on amplitude (\(T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\left(1 + \frac{1}{16}\theta_0^2 + \dots\right)\)). Christiaan Huygens discovered that a particle sliding along an inverted cycloid exhibits exact simple harmonic motion in terms of arc length \(s\): \[\ddot{s} + \left(\frac{g}{4a}\right)s = 0\] The period is independent of release height: \[T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{4a}{g}} = 4\pi\sqrt{\frac{a}{g}}\] Because the evolute of a cycloid is another cycloid, Huygens built clocks with two curved cycloidal metal plates (“cycloidal cheeks”) flanking the pendulum suspension string. When the pendulum swings wide, the flexible string wraps along the cycloidal guide, pulling the bob onto a true cycloidal path and eliminating circular timing error.

When a non-relativistic particle of charge \(q\) and mass \(m\) moves in uniform, orthogonal electric and magnetic fields (\(\mathbf{E} = E\hat{\mathbf{y}}\), \(\mathbf{B} = B\hat{\mathbf{z}}\)), its equations of motion are: \[\ddot{x} = \omega_c \dot{y}, \quad \ddot{y} = \frac{qE}{m} - \omega_c \dot{x}, \quad \omega_c = \frac{qB}{m}\] If the particle is released from rest at the origin, the solution is a pure cycloid: \[x(t) = R(\omega_c t - \sin\omega_c t), \quad y(t) = R(1 - \cos\omega_c t), \quad R = \frac{E}{\omega_c B}\] The particle accelerates along the electric field, curves under the magnetic Lorentz force, loops back to zero vertical velocity, and repeats, producing a net macroscopic drift speed: \[v_d = \frac{E}{B}\]



Conventional involute spur gears concentrate torque on small tooth contact areas and suffer from mechanical backlash. Cycloidal speed reducers use an eccentric cam driving a disc whose perimeter follows an epicycloidal/hypocycloidal profile engaging fixed ring-gear pins. Because multiple cycloidal teeth share the load simultaneously under pure rolling contact, they achieve: - Zero or near-zero backlash. - High shock load tolerance (up to 500% overload). - Compact single-stage gear ratios from \(10:1\) to \(100:1\) in robotic joint actuators and precision CNC rotary axes.



In non-linear fluid dynamics, deep-water ocean surface waves are modeled as Gerstner (trochoidal) waves. Individual water parcels do not translate horizontally; instead, each parcel executes a closed circular orbit of radius \(r(z) = r_0 e^{kz}\) around a fixed center \((x_0, z_0)\): \[x = x_0 - r_0 e^{k z_0}\sin(k x_0 - \omega t)\] \[z = z_0 + r_0 e^{k z_0}\cos(k x_0 - \omega t)\] The resulting water surface profile is a trochoid (shortened cycloid). When the wave reaches its theoretical steepness limit (\(H/\lambda = 1/\pi\)), the surface develops sharp, cusp-like peaks forming an inverted cycloid with an interior crest angle of \(120^\circ\), at which point the wave breaks.

title: Taylor Chapter 6: Calculus of Variations
text:
In classical mechanics, we often encounter problems where we need to find a path or a function that minimizes (or maximizes) a certain quantity. This is the domain of the Calculus of Variations. While ordinary calculus deals with finding points that extremize a function \(y = f(x)\), the calculus of variations deals with finding functions \(y(x)\) that extremize a functional (a function of a function), often expressed as an integral:
\[ S = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(y, y', x) \, dx \]
Two main classes of problems require this approach: 1. Symmetries make non-Cartesian coordinates (spherical, cylindrical) advantageous. 2. Constraints make it best to choose generalized coordinates (e.g., a particle on a sphere).
To transition to these generalized coordinates, Lagrangian mechanics provides a powerful framework built entirely on the calculus of variations and Hamilton’s Principle of Least Action.


The calculus of variations involves finding the minimum or maximum of a quantity that is expressible as an integral. To see how this can arise, let’s start with two simple, concrete examples.


What is the shortest path between two points \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\) in a plane? Let the path be given by a function \(y = y(x)\). An infinitesimal element of length along the path is \(ds = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2} = \sqrt{1 + (y')^2} \, dx\), where \(y' = dy/dx\).
The total length of the path is the integral: \[ L = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \sqrt{1 + [y'(x)]^2} \, dx \]
The goal is to find the function \(y(x)\) that minimizes \(L\).
(See Problem 6.1)



A similar problem is to find the path that light will follow between two points. Fermat’s principle states that the path taken by light is the one for which the time of travel is minimum (or more precisely, stationary). The time to travel a short distance \(ds\) is \(ds/v\), where \(v = c/n(x,y)\) is the speed of light in a medium with refractive index \(n(x,y)\). The total time is: \[ t = \int_1^2 \frac{ds}{v} = \frac{1}{c} \int_{x_1}^{x_2} n(x, y) \sqrt{1 + (y')^2} \, dx \] As with the shortest path, we seek a function \(y(x)\) that makes this integral stationary. In elementary calculus, a point where \(df/dx = 0\) can be a maximum, minimum, or neither. Similarly, in the calculus of variations, making an integral stationary means an infinitesimal variation of the path leaves the integral unchanged, though it doesn’t guarantee a strict minimum.




Both examples above involve an integral of the form: \[ S[y] = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(y, y', x) \, dx \] where \(S\) is a functional. We want to find the path \(y(x)\) that makes \(S\) stationary (a minimum, maximum, or saddle point).


Let the actual path that extremizes the integral be \(y(x)\). Consider a “wrong” path \(Y(x)\) that is close to \(y(x)\). We can parameterize this wrong path as: \[ Y(x) = y(x) + \alpha \eta(x) \] where \(\alpha\) is a small parameter, and \(\eta(x)\) is an arbitrary differentiable function representing the variation. Since all paths must start at \(x_1\) and end at \(x_2\), the variation must vanish at the endpoints: \[ \eta(x_1) = \eta(x_2) = 0 \]
The integral evaluated along the varied path is a function of \(\alpha\): \[ S(\alpha) = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(Y, Y', x) \, dx = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(y + \alpha \eta, y' + \alpha \eta', x) \, dx \]
For the integral to be stationary at the correct path \(y(x)\), the derivative of \(S\) with respect to \(\alpha\) must be zero when \(\alpha = 0\): \[ \left. \frac{dS}{d\alpha} \right|_{\alpha=0} = 0 \]
Using the chain rule to differentiate inside the integral: \[ \frac{dS}{d\alpha} = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial Y} \frac{\partial Y}{\partial \alpha} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial Y'} \frac{\partial Y'}{\partial \alpha} \right) dx = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial Y} \eta + \frac{\partial f}{\partial Y'} \eta' \right) dx \]
Set \(\alpha = 0\), so \(Y \to y\) and \(Y' \to y'\): \[ \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \eta(x) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \eta'(x) \right) dx = 0 \]
We integrate the second term by parts: \[ \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \eta'(x) \, dx = \left[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \eta(x) \right]_{x_1}^{x_2} - \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \right) \eta(x) \, dx \]
Since \(\eta(x_1) = \eta(x_2) = 0\), the boundary term vanishes. The condition becomes: \[ \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} - \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \right) \right] \eta(x) \, dx = 0 \]
For this to hold for any arbitrary variation \(\eta(x)\), the term in the brackets must be identically zero. This yields the Euler-Lagrange Equation:
\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} - \frac{d}{dx} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} = 0 \]
(See Problem 6.4)






For the shortest path, \(f(y, y', x) = \sqrt{1 + y'^2}\). Since \(\partial f / \partial y = 0\), the E-L equation reduces to: \[ \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} \right) = 0 \implies \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} = C \] \[ \frac{y'}{\sqrt{1 + y'^2}} = C \implies y'^2 = C^2(1 + y'^2) \implies y'^2 = \frac{C^2}{1-C^2} = m^2 \] Thus, \(y' = m\), meaning \(y = mx + b\). The shortest path is a straight line.



So far we have used \(x\) as the independent variable and \(y\) as the dependent variable. In mechanics, the independent variable is usually time \(t\), and the dependent variable is position \(x(t)\). Sometimes, as in the next example, it is more convenient to use \(y\) as the independent variable and \(x(y)\) as the dependent variable.



First posed by Johann Bernoulli in 1696. Given two points 1 and 2, with 1 higher than 2, what is the shape of a frictionless wire connecting them such that a bead released from rest at 1 slides to 2 in the minimum possible time?
Let point 1 be the origin \((0,0)\). We take the \(y\)-axis pointing downward. The speed of the bead is \(v = ds/dt\). By conservation of energy, \(E = T + U\). If released from rest at \((0,0)\), \(E = 0\). \[ \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - mgy = 0 \implies v = \sqrt{2gy} \]
The time to travel an infinitesimal distance \(ds\) is \(dt = ds/v\). The total time is: \[ t = \int_{1}^{2} \frac{ds}{v} = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{\sqrt{1 + (y')^2}}{\sqrt{2gy}} \, dx \]
We need to find the function \(y(x)\) that minimizes this time integral \(t\).
(See Problem 6.2)


For the Brachistochrone, the functional integrand is \(f(y, y') = \sqrt{\frac{1 + (y')^2}{y}}\) (dropping overall constants \(\sqrt{2g}\)).
Because \(f\) lacks explicit dependence on the independent variable \(x\) (\(\partial f / \partial x = 0\)), the Euler-Lagrange equation possesses a first integral known as the Beltrami Identity: \[ f - y' \frac{\partial f}{\partial y'} = C \]
Substituting \(f\): \[ \sqrt{\frac{1 + (y')^2}{y}} - y' \frac{y'}{\sqrt{y(1 + (y')^2)}} = C \] \[ \frac{1 + (y')^2 - (y')^2}{\sqrt{y(1 + (y')^2)}} = C \implies \frac{1}{\sqrt{y(1 + (y')^2)}} = C \implies y\big(1 + (y')^2\big) = \frac{1}{C^2} \equiv 2a \]
Solving for the derivative \(y' = dy/dx\): \[ y' = \sqrt{\frac{2a - y}{y}} \implies dx = \sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} \, dy \]
The total trajectory \(x(y)\) is given by the integral: \[ x = \int \sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} \, dy \]



Taylor introduces the parameterized substitution: \[ y = a(1 - \cos\theta) \]

Differential of the Substitution:
Differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(\theta\): \[ dy = a\sin\theta \, d\theta = 2a \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) d\theta \]
Simplifying the Radicand:
Substitute \(y = a(1 - \cos\theta)\) into the numerator and denominator:

Numerator: \(y = a(1 - \cos\theta) = 2a\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\)
Denominator: \(2a - y = 2a - a(1 - \cos\theta) = a(1 + \cos\theta) = 2a\cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\)

Taking the ratio inside the square root: \[ \frac{y}{2a - y} = \frac{2a\sin^2(\theta/2)}{2a\cos^2(\theta/2)} = \tan^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \] Assuming the motion stays within the first arch (\(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\) where \(\theta/2 \in [0, \pi]\) and \(\sin(\theta/2) \ge 0\)): \[ \sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} = \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\cos(\theta/2)} \]
Combining and Integrating:
Multiplying the simplified radical by \(dy\): \[ dx = \left(\frac{\sin(\theta/2)}{\cos(\theta/2)}\right) \cdot \left[2a \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) d\theta\right] = 2a \sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) d\theta = a(1 - \cos\theta) \, d\theta \] Integrating directly with initial condition \(x(0) = 0\) gives: \[ x(\theta) = a(\theta - \sin\theta), \quad y(\theta) = a(1 - \cos\theta) \] These are the parametric equations of a cycloid.





Mathematical Reason (Principal Square Root):
The square root identity is \(\sqrt{u^2} = |u|\). Thus: \[ \sqrt{\tan^2(\theta/2)} = |\tan(\theta/2)| = \frac{|\sin(\theta/2)|}{|\cos(\theta/2)|} \] Within the first arch (\(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\)), the half-angle satisfies \(\frac{\theta}{2} \in [0, \pi]\), where the sine function is unconditionally non-negative: \[ \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \ge 0 \implies \left|\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right| = \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) \] This eliminates piece-wise absolute value signs without ambiguity. Along the descending branch (\(\theta < \pi\)), \(\cos(\theta/2) > 0\) and \(dy > 0\). Past the trough (\(\theta > \pi\)), \(\cos(\theta/2) < 0\) while the particle ascends (\(dy < 0\)), maintaining consistent directional progress \(dx \ge 0\).
Physical Reason (Energy Bounds & Uniqueness):

Energy Ceiling: By conservation of energy, \(v = \sqrt{2gy}\). At \(y = 0\), speed vanishes (\(v = 0\)). The bead cannot ascend into \(y < 0\), ensuring the trajectory cannot continue past the cusp at \(\theta = 2\pi\).
Path Uniqueness: By scaling the radius \(a\) and endpoint angle \(\theta_2 \in (0, 2\pi]\), a unique single cycloid arch connects the origin \((0, 0)\) to any target point \((x_2, y_2)\) with \(x_2 > 0, y_2 \ge 0\).
No Redundant Loops: Any path spanning into subsequent arches would entail climbing to a cusp, arresting, and falling through extra dips, adding superfluous travel time and violating \(\delta T = 0\).





Taylor calls \(y = a(1 - \cos\theta)\) an “unlikely looking substitution,” but it is completely systematic.
Rationalizing the numerator: \[ \sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} = \frac{y}{\sqrt{y(2a - y)}} = \frac{y}{\sqrt{2ay - y^2}} \] Completing the square in the denominator: \[ 2ay - y^2 = a^2 - (y - a)^2 \implies \int \frac{y}{\sqrt{a^2 - (y - a)^2}} \, dy \]
Geometric Origin:
The expression \(\sqrt{a^2 - (y - a)^2}\) describes a semicircle \((y - a)^2 + w^2 = a^2\) of radius \(a\) centered at \((0, a)\).
Dual Circle Parameterizations:
Any form \(\sqrt{a^2 - u^2}\) permits two standard circular substitutions: 1. Sine substitution (\(u = a\sin\phi\)): Setting \(y - a = a\sin\phi \implies y = a(1 + \sin\phi)\). At the release point \(y = 0\), \(\sin\phi = -1 \implies \phi = -\pi/2\), imposing an unwanted phase shift. 2. Inverted cosine substitution (\(u = -a\cos\theta\)): Setting \(y - a = -a\cos\theta \implies y = a(1 - \cos\theta)\). At release (\(y = 0\)), \(\cos(0) = 1 \implies \theta = 0\), matching initial rest conditions at the origin with zero phase offset!



Rather than guessing a trigonometric form, set the entire linear radical equal to an algebraic variable \(u\): \[ u = \sqrt{\frac{y}{2a - y}} \implies y = \frac{2a u^2}{1 + u^2}, \quad dy = \frac{4a u}{(1 + u^2)^2} \, du \] The integral becomes: \[ x = \int u \, dy = 4a \int \frac{u^2}{(1 + u^2)^2} \, du \]
This can be evaluated via two direct methods:


Decomposing as \(u \cdot \frac{u}{(1 + u^2)^2}\) with \(f = u\) and \(dg = \frac{u}{(1 + u^2)^2}du \implies g = -\frac{1}{2(1 + u^2)}\): \[ \int \frac{u^2}{(1 + u^2)^2} \, du = -\frac{u}{2(1 + u^2)} + \frac{1}{2}\int \frac{du}{1 + u^2} = -\frac{u}{2(1 + u^2)} + \frac{1}{2}\arctan(u) \] Multiplying by \(4a\) and enforcing \(x(0) = 0\): \[ x(u) = 2a\arctan(u) - \frac{2a u}{1 + u^2} \] Setting \(u = \tan(\theta/2)\), we find \(\arctan(u) = \theta/2\) and \(\frac{2u}{1 + u^2} = \sin\theta\), which directly recovers: \[ x(\theta) = a(\theta - \sin\theta), \quad y(\theta) = a(1 - \cos\theta) \]



Substituting \(u = \tan\phi\) with \(du = \sec^2\phi \, d\phi\): \[ 4a \int \frac{\tan^2\phi}{\sec^4\phi}\sec^2\phi \, d\phi = 4a \int \sin^2\phi \, d\phi = 2a(\phi - \sin\phi\cos\phi) \] Setting \(\theta = 2\phi\) immediately produces \(x = a(\theta - \sin\theta)\).




The parameter \(\theta\) is the cumulative rotation angle (in radians) of a wheel of radius \(a\) rolling without slipping along the underside of the horizontal axis (\(y = 0\)):
